title: What the Fed fears most is not tariffs but unanchored inflation expectations
dek: Chicago Fed President Goolsbee identifies the biggest risk as inflation: after five and a half years above target, the AI narrative may push rates up in the short term rather than down; his key advice for rate-sensitive industries is to watch the data, not the stock market.
why: A frontline policymaker rarely offers actionable quantitative anchors: the terminal rate is roughly 3%, but only if inflation returns to 2%; he also offers contrarian takes on the AI bubble and job-loss panic.
who: Founders, CFOs, and investors concerned about funding costs and interest rate trends; those planning AI capital expenditures or hiring decisions.
skip: The opening ad and Jackson Hole travel pleasantries (first ~4 minutes) can be fast-forwarded; the core is in the middle and later sections.

points.h: 19 chairs are not for consensus but for argument
points.body: He explains why the FOMC is worth keeping with 12 regional Fed presidents plus 7 Board governors, totaling 19 chairs: not for consensus, but to let different worldviews collide under high uncertainty. Goolsbee says colleagues can shout at him and can change his interpretation of data. This structure insulates rate decisions from the political cycle as much as possible, because the 14-year staggered terms mean no one can replace the whole table at once. The direct lesson for founders: when making major judgments, surround yourself with people who dare to push back, not an echo chamber.

points.h: The Fed's real fear is not price hikes but unanchored expectations
points.body: The real danger of tariff and oil price shocks is not a one-time price increase but making people believe high inflation will persist. Once such expectations form, workers demand 6% wages, businesses price at 7%, and the Fed must use a deep recession to break expectations if it wants to bring inflation down. Goolsbee calls this 'unanchoring of inflation expectations' and says it is the self-fulfilling mechanism he is most vigilant about. For entrepreneurs, this logic means: whether a cost increase is one-off matters more than how much costs rise.

points.h: Five and a half years above target, the Fed's own record is not pretty
points.body: Goolsbee admits the Fed's performance has not been pretty: nearly six years, at least five and a half of them above the 2% target, with a recent reversal in the past year. He cites on-the-ground observations from the Seventh District (Midwest): businesses say input costs have surged, farmers say selling prices are not rising but costs are crushing, and everyone talks about affordability. His conclusion: with the public highly sensitive to prices, any new supply shock—tariffs, Middle East oil prices, chip shortages, AI data centers—is more likely to be interpreted as long-term inflation.

points.h: The new chair is pulling back the Fed's forward guidance
points.body: New Chair Kevin Walsh is overhauling the Fed's communication style: he dislikes 'forward guidance'—the explicit promise that 'if X happens, we will hike or cut.' Goolsbee observes that FOMC statements have become noticeably shorter, and Walsh has set up five working groups covering inflation, AI and productivity, the balance sheet, and other areas, staffed with well-known people he trusts. Reports are not out yet, but they could become Walsh's signature reform. Markets must adapt: the Fed will make fewer promises, and future expectation volatility may be higher.

points.h: Replacing people to influence rates is the red line for independence
points.body: Goolsbee divides today's pressures into two types: personal attacks on Powell, Lisa Cook, and others, including criminal investigations and attempts to remove them; and direct demands to 'cut rates.' He says the Fed's independence has traditionally been narrowly defined—setting rates without political interference. Once an administration tries to influence rates by replacing people, 'any economist would see that as a problem.' He does not go all the way, but this is his clearest statement to the White House.

points.h: AI is a reason to hike rates in the short term, not cut them
points.body: He first cools the AI narrative with district facts: manufacturing has the highest share in the entire Fed system, but companies are still looking for use cases and complaining that tokens are too expensive; productivity growth, after a two-and-a-half-year pickup, has shown about six months of weakness. Then he offers a counterintuitive judgment: if everyone simultaneously pours money into data centers, betting with IPOs or expected future earnings, the short-term economy will overheat. The central bank's daily job is to prevent overheating, not to judge whether AI will revolutionize things in 20 years, so AI's short-term policy implication may be to push rates up, not down.

points.h: AI taking all jobs is the lump of labor fallacy
points.body: He attributes the narrative that 'AI will make everyone unemployed' to the lump of labor fallacy: treating the total amount of labor as a fixed stone that, once AI surpasses it, leaves no new jobs for people. He says this claim has been proven wrong every time in the past; he admits 'maybe this time is different,' but he is willing to bet the opposite: in 20 years there will not be 95% unemployment, nor will only six people own all AI companies. He positions himself as a 'grim optimist'—not shying away from short-term pain but optimistic about long-term income growth.

points.h: The terminal rate is roughly 3%, provided inflation turns around
points.body: Goolsbee offers a rare quantitative anchor: his personal loose view is that if inflation returns to a 2% path, rates will converge to the neutral rate (what he calls star), roughly 3% nominal rate = 2% inflation + 1% real rate. But the precondition is that inflation must turn downward; the past five and a half years have been above target, and the last year has been moving in the wrong direction. For rate-sensitive industries, his advice is to watch data and inflation, not the stock market—the people around the FOMC table discuss the real economy, and the stock market is only a secondary reference.
